hints.text: Two litres is the gap between 8 and two fives.
Fill the 5 and pour it into the 8, twice.
Fill 5, pour into 8, fill 5, pour into 8 until it is full: 2 litres stay in the 5.

feedback.correct: Four steps: fill, pour, fill, pour.
feedback.generic: Not there yet. Try filling the 5 and pouring it into the 8 twice.

explain.text: Fill the 5 and pour it into the 8, then fill the 5 again. Pouring until the 8 is full moves only 3 litres, so 2 stay behind. A search of every state finds no route shorter than these 4 steps.

screens.title: Jugs of 4 and 9
screens.prose: Now a 4-litre jug and a 9-litre jug, and the tap. Each fill, empty or pour is one step.
screens.question: What is the fewest steps that leaves 6 litres in a jug?

hints.text: Six is 9 minus 3. How can you get a 3, or a gap of 3?
Fill the 9 and pour into the 4 twice: 1 litre is left in the 9.
Move that 1 litre into the 4, fill the 9, and top up the 4: 6 stay in the 9.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a route, then try to shorten it.

byKey.six: No route of 6 steps exists; a search of every state finds 8 at least.
byKey.four: Four steps can make 1 or 8 litres, but not 6.
byKey.ten: A route of 10 works, but a shorter one takes 8.

explain.text: Fill 9, pour into 4, empty 4, pour again: 1 litre is left in the 9. Empty the 4, move the 1 litre into it, fill 9 and top up the 4, leaving 6. A search finds nothing shorter than 8 steps.

screens.title: Two ropes, unevenly
screens.prose: Two ropes each burn for 80 minutes, but unevenly: half the length need not take half the time. Light rope A at both ends and rope B at one end. When A goes out, light B's other end.

state.caption: Rope A from both ends, rope B from one end.

screens.question: When does rope B go out, in minutes?

hints.text: When does rope A go out?
Burning from both ends, A is gone at 40 minutes.
B then has 40 minutes of burn left, and both ends halve it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find what B has left when A goes out.

byKey.eighty: That ignores the second flame on B. Its last 40 minutes of burn take 20.
byKey.forty: That is when A goes out. B still has 40 minutes of burn left.
byKey.onetwenty: You added B's full time after A. B was already burning from the start.

explain.text: Rope A, lit at both ends, is gone at 40 minutes, and B has 40 minutes of burn left. Lit at both ends, that remainder takes 20, so B goes out at 60. Principle: lighting both ends halves whatever burn time is left.

canvas.caption: B's last 40 minutes of burn take 20: it goes out at 60.

screens.title: The rope plan in order
screens.prose: Put the plan for measuring 60 minutes in order. One line does not belong.
screens.question: Order the steps.

lines.text: Light rope A at both ends and rope B at one end, together.
Rope A goes out at 40 minutes.
At that moment, light the other end of rope B.
Rope B's last 40 minutes of burn now take 20.
Rope B goes out at 60 minutes.
Cut rope B in half and burn one half from one end.
lines.why: The burn is uneven, so half the length is not half the time.

hints.text: Only an event, a rope going out, can trigger the next step.
A going out at 40 is the trigger for the second flame on B.
Light, A goes out, light B's other end, halve the remainder, B goes out.

feedback.correct: Light, wait for A, light B again, B goes out at 60.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step waits for an event.

byKey.d1: Cutting a rope measures length, not time. The burn is uneven.
byKey.left-out: Every line except cutting the rope belongs.

explain.text: A rope going out is the only clock, so each step waits for one. The second flame on B halves its remaining 40 minutes. Principle: chain events, and halve what is left with a second flame.

screens.title: Forty minutes from one rope
screens.prose: One rope burns for 80 minutes, unevenly. A candidate says: cut it in half and burn one piece.

state.caption: One rope, 80 minutes from one end.

screens.question: How do you measure 40 minutes with it?

options.text: Cut it in half and burn one piece
options.why: You cut by length. The burn is uneven, so one half may burn for 70 minutes.

options.text: Light one end and stop when half the length has burnt
options.why: You watched the length. Half the length can take any part of the 80 minutes.

options.text: Light one end and wait 40 minutes
options.why: You have no clock: the rope is the only one.

hints.text: What is the only thing you can rely on about the rope?
Its total burn is 80 minutes, whatever the pace along it.
Two flames burn the whole rope between them, meeting when 80 minutes of burn are used: after 40.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the total burn time, not the length.

byKey.cut: Cutting measures length, and the burn is uneven.
byKey.half: Half the length is not half the time.
byKey.mark: Waiting 40 minutes needs a clock, and the rope is your only one.

explain.text: Two flames use up the rope's 80 minutes of burn between them, so they meet after 40. Where they meet along the rope does not matter. Principle: use the total time, never the length.

screens.title: Jugs of 6 and 9
screens.prose: A tap, a 6-litre jug and a 9-litre jug.
screens.question: Can you ever measure exactly 4 litres?

options.why: You trusted more steps. Every amount stays a multiple of 3.

options.text: Yes: 9 minus 6 is 3, and 3 plus 1 is 4
options.why: No step makes 1. Fills, empties and pours keep multiples of 3.

hints.text: What do 6 and 9 have in common?
Both are multiples of 3.
Every fill, empty and pour keeps both jugs at multiples of 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the amounts modulo 3.

byKey.long: Every amount stays a multiple of 3, however many steps.

explain.text: A fill or an empty sets a jug to a multiple of 3. A pour moves a multiple of 3, so every amount stays a multiple of $\gcd(6, 9) = 3$. Principle: the gcd is an invariant, and 4 is not a multiple of it.

screens.title: States, gcd and events
screens.prose: Each time you wrote the states and searched from the start. For jugs of $a$ and $b$ litres, the amounts you can make are the multiples of the gcd. $$\{\, k\gcd(a, b) : 0 < k\gcd(a, b) \le \max(a, b) \,\}.$$ For ropes and hourglasses, the only clock is an event.
screens.question: Which amounts can jugs of 6 and 15 litres leave in a jug? Select all that apply.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The gcd of 6 and 15 is 3.

explain.text: The gcd of 6 and 15 is 3, so every amount is a multiple of 3 up to 15. A search reaches each of 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15. Amounts such as 4 and 10 never appear.

screens.title: Drill: thirteen minutes
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. You have a 5-minute and a 9-minute hourglass. You may turn either over whenever one of them empties.
screens.question: Order the steps that measure 13 minutes. One line does not belong.

lines.text: At 5 minutes the 5 empties; turn it over.
At 9 minutes the 9 empties; the 5 has run 4 minutes since its turn.
Turn the 5 over: its 4 minutes of sand run back.
At 9 minutes, turn the 9 over and stop it after 4 minutes.
lines.why: Nothing marks 4 minutes on the 9. Use the sand already in the 5.

hints.text: 13 is 9 plus 4. Where can you find 4 minutes of sand?
When the 9 empties, the 5 has been running for 4 minutes since its turn.
Turn the 5 at 9 minutes and those 4 minutes run back.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each turn happens when a glass empties.

byKey.d1: You cannot stop a glass at 4 minutes without a clock. Use the 5's sand.
byKey.left-out: Every line except stopping the 9 belongs.

explain.text: Start both and turn the 5 when it empties at 5. At 9 the 9 empties and the 5 has 4 minutes of sand below; turning it gives 13. Principle: sand that has run is a stored time you can run back.

screens.title: Drill: two ropes, every mark
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes. Two ropes each burn for 80 minutes, unevenly. You may light ends only at the start or when a rope goes out.
screens.question: Which moments, counted from when you first light a rope, can you mark? Select all that apply.

options.why: 20 is the gap between 40 and 60, not a moment counted from the start.
The first event comes at 40 at the earliest, with both ends lit.
100 needs a flame lit at 40 and another at 80. The first rope ends at 40 or at 80, not both.

hints.text: Events happen only when a rope goes out. What can the first rope give?
40 with both ends lit, or 80 with one.
The second rope adds 60 (second flame at 40), 120 (lit at 40, or both ends at 80) or 160.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List every event the two ropes can make, from the first lighting.

explain.text: The first rope ends at 40 or 80. The second rope then adds 60, 80, 120 or 160, and a search of every plan finds no other mark. Principle: list the events, because the events are the only clock.

screens.title: Drill: nine minutes
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes. A 4-minute and a 7-minute hourglass. Two of the lines below happen at the same moment, so they may swap.
screens.question: Order the steps that measure 9 minutes.

lines.text: At 4 minutes the 4 empties; turn it over.
At 7 minutes the 7 empties; turn it over.
At 8 minutes the 7 has run 1 minute since its turn.
Turn the 7 over: that 1 minute runs back, ending at 9.

hints.text: Nine is 8 plus 1. Where is 1 minute of sand at 8 minutes?
The 7 was turned at 7, so at 8 it has 1 minute of sand below.
Turn it at 8 and that minute runs back: 9.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each turn waits for a glass to empty.

explain.text: The 4 marks 4 and 8, and the 7 turned at 7 holds 1 minute of run sand at 8. Turning it then runs that minute back, ending at 9. Principle: two glasses make new times from the gaps between their events.

screens.title: No tap
screens.prose: Follow-up. The interviewer takes the tap away. A full 10-litre jug and empty jugs of 7 and 3 litres. Split the water into two lots of 5 litres. Only pours are allowed.
screens.question: Reach 5 litres in the 10 and 5 in the 7.

hints.text: Use the 3-litre jug as a measure, moving water round in a cycle.
Pour 10 into 7. Then pour 7 into 3, and empty the 3 into the 10 each time it fills.
When the 7 runs dry, refill it from the 10. Stop when the 10 and the 7 hold 5 each.

feedback.generic: Not there yet. Pour 7 into 3, empty each full 3 into the 10, and refill the 7 when it runs dry.

explain.text: Pour 7 into 3, tip each full 3 into the 10, and refill an empty 7. The route passes 3, 7, 0 and 9, 1, 0 on its way to 5, 5, 0. Principle: without a tap the total is fixed, so the states are the ways to split 10.

screens.title: The fewest pours
screens.prose: Same jugs: a full 10, empty 7 and 3, no tap.
screens.question: What is the fewest pours that splits the water into two lots of 5?

hints.text: Search from the start, shortest first.
Pouring 10 into 7 first leads to 3, 7, 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Search the states from the start, shortest first.

byKey.seven: No route of 7 pours exists; a search finds 9 at least.
byKey.ten: That route works, but one pour can be saved: the shortest takes 9.
byKey.eleven: A route of 11 works but is not the shortest. Starting with 10 into 3 takes 10 at best; 10 into 7 first takes 9.

explain.text: A search of every split from 10, 0, 0 finds 5, 5, 0 first at depth 9. The route goes 3, 7, 0, then 3, 4, 3, 6, 4, 0 and on to 5, 5, 0. Principle: shortest first finds the fewest steps.

ideas: Write the states, such as jug contents, and search from the start, shortest first.
Jugs of $a$ and $b$ litres make exactly the multiples of $\gcd(a, b)$ up to the larger jug.
For ropes and hourglasses the only clock is an event; a second flame halves the burn left.

formula.name: Jug amounts
formula.note: Jugs of 6 and 9 make 3, 6 and 9, never 4.

summary.trap: Cutting a rope in half does not halve its time: the burn is uneven. Light both ends.

quiz.prose: A tap, a 3-litre jug and a 7-litre jug.
quiz.question: What is the fewest steps that leaves 5 litres in a jug?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Search from the start, shortest first.

byKey.four: Four steps can make 1 or 6 litres, but not 5.
byKey.six: No route of 6 steps leaves 5 litres; the shortest takes 8.
byKey.ten: Ten works, but 8 is the fewest.

explain.text: Fill 7, pour into 3, empty 3, pour again: 1 litre is left in the 7. Empty the 3, move the 1 litre into it, fill 7 and top up the 3, leaving 5. A search finds nothing shorter than 8 steps.

quiz.prose: A tap, a 4-litre jug and a 6-litre jug.
quiz.question: Can you measure exactly 3 litres?

options.text: Yes: 6 minus 4 is 2, and 2 plus 1 is 3
options.why: No step makes 1 litre. Every amount stays even.

options.text: Yes: fill the 6 and pour half out
options.why: Without marks you cannot pour exactly half.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the gcd of 4 and 6.

byKey.yes: Every amount stays a multiple of 2.
byKey.half: Half a jug cannot be judged without marks.

explain.text: Every fill, empty and pour keeps both jugs at multiples of $\gcd(4, 6) = 2$. Three is odd, so never. Principle: the gcd bounds what jugs can measure.

quiz.prose: Two ropes each burn for 60 minutes, unevenly.
quiz.question: What is the shortest time you can mark, counted from when you first light a rope?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The first event comes when a rope goes out.

byKey.fifteen: Fifteen would need a quarter of a rope's burn, and you can only halve with two ends.
byKey.sixty: Light both ends of one rope: it goes out at 30.

explain.text: The earliest event is a rope lit at both ends going out, after 30 minutes. Nothing goes out sooner, since each rope has at most two flames. Principle: the first event bounds the shortest mark.
